title: What If You Could Breathe Underwater?

sources.title: American Museum of Natural History: Life in Water, Vertebrates - Breathing
FAO: Water quality, dissolved oxygen (fish culture manual)
Scientific American (1968): Altered mice breathe water instead of air
Springer review chapter: Liquid ventilation, history and clinical use

scenes.narration: Imagine you dive into the ocean, open your mouth, and just breathe the water, like a fish.
Subscribe for more weird biology. Now, the catch.
A liter of air holds about two hundred ten milliliters of oxygen. A liter of water holds around eight. That's over twenty times less.
And water is nearly eight hundred times denser than air, and a hundred times thicker. Pumping it in and out of your lungs would be brutal work.
Fish solve this with gills, pulling out about seventy-five percent of the oxygen flowing past, twice what our lungs take from a breath.
But here's the twist. In 1961, a scientist named Johannes Kylstra had mice breathe salt water loaded with oxygen under high pressure. And they did.
What limited them wasn't oxygen. It was getting rid of carbon dioxide fast enough.
Later, doctors swapped water for special oxygen-rich liquids, and in 1989 tested them in the lungs of premature babies.
So humans can breathe a liquid. Just not the ocean.

claims.claim: Air contains about 209-210 mL of oxygen per liter
Water holds roughly 5-8 mL of dissolved oxygen per liter, about 20-40 times less than air depending on temperature
Water is about 777 times denser and 100 times more viscous than air
Fish gills extract about 75% of the oxygen passing through, twice the percentage our lungs take from air
Kylstra's mice breathed oxygenated saline under high pressure (8 atm) in experiments at Leiden from 1961
The limiting factor was eliminating carbon dioxide, not lack of oxygen
Mice breathed isotonic saline equilibrated with oxygen at 8 atm
First clinical trial of perfluorocarbon liquid ventilation in neonates was in 1989

meta.title: What If You Could Breathe Underwater?
meta.summary: Water holds a tiny fraction of the oxygen in air and is far heavier to pump. Yet in 1961 mice really did breathe oxygenated water, and the real problem turned out to be carbon dioxide.
